# Upper arm and elbow

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Basics of rheumatology > Upper arm and elbow*

[Original Article Link](/library/TL06Cg)

---

## Summary

The upper arm, or brachium, extends between the <u>shoulder joint</u> and <u>elbow</u>. The <u>shoulder joint</u> connects the upper arm to the torso and the <u>shoulder girdle</u>, while the <u>elbow joint</u> connects it to the forearm. The muscles of the upper arm move the <u>elbow joint</u> (<u>flexion</u> and extension) and the forearm (<u>pronation</u> and <u>supination</u>), as well as stabilize and move the <u>shoulder joint</u> (<u>internal rotation</u> and <u>flexion</u>). This article covers the bones, muscles, vasculature, <u>lymphatics</u>, and innervation of the upper arm and <u>elbow</u>.




See “<u>Forearm, wrist, and hand</u>” and “Shoulder, <u>axilla</u>, and <u>brachial plexus</u>.”

---

## Humerus

### Definition




The humerus is a bone of the arm that articulates proximally with the <u>scapula</u> to form the <u>shoulder joint</u> and distally with the radius and <u>ulna</u> to form the <u>elbow joint</u>.




![Humerus](media/t7pafgv38n6vthqzgcwttjr2.jpg)

Humerus




### Head of the humerus



* Spherical <u>proximal</u> portion of the <u>humerus</u> that articulates with the <u>glenoid cavity</u> of the <u>scapula</u> (i.e., the ball of the ball-and-socket <u>glenohumeral joint</u>)




### Neck of the humerus




* Anatomical neck of the humerus: constriction that separates the <u>head of the humerus</u> from the tubercles and allows attachment of the <u>ligaments</u> of the <u>glenohumeral joint</u>

* Surgical neck of the humerus

* Constriction below the tubercles

* The <u>axillary nerve</u> and <u>posterior humeral circumflex artery</u> pass around the <u>dorsal</u> part of the <u>surgical neck of the humerus</u> together.

* Greater tubercle of the humerus: site of insertion of the <u>supraspinatus</u>, <u>infraspinatus</u>, and <u>teres minor</u> of the <u>rotator cuff</u>

* Lesser tubercle of the humerus: site of insertion of the <u>subscapularis</u> of the <u>rotator cuff</u>

* Bicipital groove (<u>intertubercular sulcus</u>): deep groove between the tubercles in which the <u>tendon</u> of the long head of <u>biceps brachii</u> lie (site of insertion for <u>pectoralis major</u>, <u>teres major</u>, and <u>latissimus dorsi</u>)





### Shaft of the humerus




* Deltoid tuberosity: a rough area on the superolateral aspect of the <u>shaft of the humerus</u> into which the deltoid is inserted

* Radial groove: groove on the mid-posterolateral surface of the shaft in which the <u>radial nerve</u> and <u>deep brachial artery</u> run together

* <u>Distal</u> <u>humerus</u> (<u>medial</u> to <u>lateral</u>)

* Medial epicondyle: <u>medial</u>-most bony prominence of the <u>humerus</u> (site of origin of most forearm flexors and <u>pronator teres</u>)

* Ulnar groove

* Deep groove below the <u>medial epicondyle</u> through which the <u>ulnar nerve</u> passes

* Funny bone: Bumping the <u>ulnar nerve</u> against the <u>medial epicondyle</u> causes <u>pain</u> or a tingling, <u>shock</u>-like sensation and numbness in the distribution of the <u>ulnar nerve</u> (forearm, palm, and <u>palmar</u> sides of digits IV and V).

* Humeral trochlea; : a dumbbell-shaped bony projection that articulates with the <u>ulna</u>

* Coronoid fossa; : <u>depression</u> above the trochlea on the <u>ventral</u> <u>humerus</u> that receives the <u>coronoid process</u> of the <u>ulna</u> when the forearm is flexed

* Capitulum; : spherical bony prominence that articulates with the <u>head of the radius</u>

* Radial fossa; : <u>depression</u> above the <u>capitulum</u> on the <u>ventral</u> <u>humerus</u> that receives the <u>head of the radius</u> when the forearm is flexed

* Lateral epicondyle: <u>lateral</u>-most bony prominence (site of origin of most forearm extensors and supinator)

* Olecranon fossa; : bony <u>depression</u> on the <u>dorsal</u> aspect of the <u>distal</u> <u>humerus</u> (receives the <u>olecranon process</u> of the <u>ulna</u> when the forearm is extended)





> [!NOTE]
> “Broken ARM:” the Axillary, Radial, and Median nerves can be injured as a result of a <u>humerus fracture</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Tendinosis</u> at the <u>medial epicondyle</u> (<u>medial epicondylitis</u>) is called <u>golfer's elbow</u>. <u>Tendinosis</u> at the <u>lateral epicondyle</u> (<u>lateral epicondylitis</u>) is called <u>tennis elbow</u>.References:[[1]](/library/vjYAX6)

## Muscles

The muscles of the arm can be categorized into two groups: flexors and extensors. They lie deep to the brachial <u>fascia</u> and are divided into <u>anterior</u> (flexor) and <u>posterior</u> (extensor) compartments by the <u>medial</u> intermuscular septum and the <u>lateral</u> intermuscular septum.




For specific tests to assess the function of these muscles, see “<u>Motor function</u>” in “<u>Neurological examination</u>.”




### Anterior compartment of the arm (flexors)




The <u>anterior</u> compartment contains three muscles that are <u>elbow</u> flexors, all of which are innervated by the <u>musculocutaneous nerve</u>.




| Overview of the <u>muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muscle | <br>Biceps brachii<br> | Brachialis | <br>Coracobrachialis <br> |
| Origin | <br><br>* Long head of the biceps: <u>supraglenoid tubercle</u> of the <u>scapula</u><br><br>* Short head of the <u>biceps</u>: <u>coracoid process</u> of the <u>scapula</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Shaft of humerus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Coracoid process</u> of the <u>scapula</u><br><br> |
| Insertion | <br>* <u>Radial tuberosity</u><br><br> | <br>* Ulnar tuberosity<br><br> | <br>* Upper third of the <u>medial</u> <u>shaft of the humerus</u><br><br> |
| Innervation | <br>* <u>Musculocutaneous nerve</u> (C5–C7)<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Function <br> | <br><br>* <u>Elbow</u>: <u>flexion</u><br><br>* Forearm: <u>supination</u> (strongest supinator)<br><br>* Shoulder: <u>internal rotation</u> and <u>flexion</u><br><br>* Long head: shoulder <u>abduction</u><br><br>* Short head: shoulder <u>adduction</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Elbow</u>: <u>flexion</u><br><br> | <br>* Shoulder: arm <u>flexion</u>, <u>adduction</u> (weak)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The <u>elbow</u> flexors are innervated by the <u>musculocutaneous nerve</u>.

### Posterior compartment of the arm (extensors)




The <u>posterior</u> compartment contains two muscles that are <u>elbow</u> extensors, both of which are innervated by the <u>radial nerve</u>.




| Overview of the <u>muscles of the posterior compartment of the arm</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Muscle | <br>Triceps brachii<br> | Anconeus muscle |
| Origin | <br><br>* Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of the <u>scapula</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> head: <u>shaft of the humerus</u>, above the <u>radial groove</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u> head: <u>shaft of the humerus</u>, below the <u>radial groove</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u><br><br> |
| Insertion | <br>* <u>Olecranon process</u> of the <u>ulna</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Dorsal</u> ulnar surface <u>distal</u> of the <u>olecranon</u><br><br> |
| Innervation | <br>* <u>Radial nerve</u> (C6–C8)<br><br> |  |
| Function | <br><br>* Shoulder: <u>adduction</u> and extension<br><br>* <u>Elbow</u>: extension<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Elbow</u>: extension<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The <u>elbow</u> extensors are innervated by the <u>radial nerve</u>.

### Muscle grooves of the arm




There are two bicipital grooves between the muscle groups of the arm that serve as channels for important neurovascular pathways. They are different from the <u>bicipital groove</u> that lies between the tubercles of the <u>humerus</u>.




|  | Medial bicipital groove | Lateral bicipital groove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location | <br>* Between the <u>biceps brachii muscle</u> and the <u>triceps brachii</u><br><br> | <br>* Between the <u>biceps brachii muscle</u> and <u>brachialis muscle</u><br><br> |
| <u>Arteries</u> | <br>* <u>Brachial artery</u><br><br> | <br>* Radial collateral <u>artery</u><br><br> |
| <u>Veins</u> | <br><br>* <u>Basilic vein</u><br><br>* <u>Brachial veins</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Radial collateral <u>vein</u><br><br>* <u>Cephalic vein</u><br><br><br> |
| Nerves | <br><br>* <u>Ulnar nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Median nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Radial nerve</u><br><br> |

## Vasculature and lymphatics

### Arterial supply




The brachial artery is the main <u>artery</u> of the arm, forearm, and hand.




* Origin: : inferolateral border of the <u>teres major</u> (continuation of the <u>axillary artery</u>)

* Course

* Lies in the <u>medial</u> aspect of the arm, in close proximity to the <u>median nerve</u>

* Ends with bifurcation into the <u>radial artery</u> and <u>ulnar artery</u> just below the <u>cubital fossa</u>

* Branches

* Deep brachial artery;  (profunda brachii): supplies the <u>triceps</u> muscle

* Small branches to the <u>elbow anastomosis</u> (the superior and inferior ulnar collateral <u>arteries</u>)

* Terminal branches (See “Vasculature and <u>lymphatics</u>” in “<u>Forearm, wrist, and hand</u>”): <u>ulnar artery</u> and <u>radial artery</u> which supply the forearm and hand





> [!TIP]
> The <u>brachial artery</u> can be compressed proximally against the <u>medial</u> <u>humerus</u> to stop bleeding in the <u>distal</u> arm.




![Arteries of the upper extremity](media/pczabpv1mfqwjuigejhxhtfp.jpg)

Arteries of the upper extremity




### Venous drainage




* <u>Superficial veins</u> (See “<u>Veins</u>” in “<u>Forearm, wrist, and hand</u>”)

* <u>Cephalic vein</u>

* <u>Basilic vein</u>

* <u>Deep veins</u>: brachial veins (a pair of <u>veins</u> that accompany the <u>brachial artery</u>)

* Tributaries: ulnar vein and radial vein

* Unite with the <u>basilic vein</u> at the outer border of <u>teres major</u> to form the <u>axillary vein</u>





![Veins of the upper extremity](media/bl2j6lljsiu87rm2l3rbn7wd.jpg)

Veins of the upper extremity




### <u>Lymphatic drainage</u>




* The <u>lymphatics</u> follow the <u>superficial</u> and <u>deep veins</u>.

* The <u>lateral</u> aspect of the upper limb is drained by <u>lymphatics</u> that follow the <u>cephalic vein</u> and ultimately drain into the <u>lateral</u> and infraclavicular <u>lymph nodes</u>.

* The <u>medial</u> aspect of the upper limb is drained by <u>lymphatics</u> that accompany the <u>basilic vein</u> and ultimately drain into the <u>lateral</u> <u>axillary lymph nodes</u>.

### Motor and sensory innervation of the arm and <u>elbow</u>




| <br>Overview of the innervation of the arm and <u>elbow</u> <br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Function | Nerve | Innervated structures |
| Motor | <br>* <u>Musculocutaneous nerve</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm</u>: <u>biceps brachii</u>, <u>brachialis</u>, <u>coracobrachialis</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Radial nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Muscles of the posterior compartment of the arm</u>: <u>triceps brachii</u>, <u>anconeus</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> part of the <u>brachialis</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Sensory <br> | <br>* Medial brachial cutaneous nerve (branch of <u>medial</u> cord of <u>brachial plexus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Inferomedial aspect of the arm<br><br> |
| <br>* Superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve (branch of the <u>axillary nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Inferior aspect of the deltoid<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve (branch of the <u>radial nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Inferolateral aspect of the arm<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Posterior brachial cutaneous nerve (branch of the <u>radial nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Distal</u> third of the <u>posterior</u> arm<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Intercostobrachial nerve (branch of the second <u>intercostal nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Proximal</u> half of the <u>medial</u> arm<br><br> |  |





See “<u>Nerve injuries in the upper body</u>” in “<u>Peripheral nerve injuries</u>” and “<u>Motor function</u>” and “Sensation” in “<u>Neurological examination</u>.”

### <u>Dermatomal</u> distribution of the arm




* <u>Proximal</u> shoulder: C4

* <u>Lateral</u> arm: C5

* <u>Posterior</u> arm (<u>elbow</u>): C6

* Inferomedial arm: T1

* Superomedial arm: T2

## Elbow joint

* Type of <u>joint</u>

* Complex synovial <u>hinge joint</u> between the <u>distal</u> end of the <u>humerus</u> and the <u>proximal</u> ends of the radius (<u>humeroradial joint</u>) and <u>ulna</u> (<u>humeroulnar joint</u>), as well as between the radius and <u>ulna</u> (<u>radioulnar joint</u>)

* Connects the arm and forearm

* Composition: consists of three articulations 

* Humeroulnar joint: articulation between the <u>trochlear notch</u> of the <u>ulna</u> and the <u>trochlea of the humerus</u> that allows <u>elbow</u> <u>flexion</u>/extension

* Humeroradial joint: articulation between the <u>head of the radius</u> and the <u>capitulum of the humerus</u> that allows forearm <u>pronation</u>/<u>supination</u>

* Proximal radioulnar joint: articulation between the <u>head of the radius</u> and <u>proximal</u> <u>ulna</u> that allows forearm <u>pronation</u>/<u>supination</u>

* <u>Ligaments</u>

* Radial collateral ligament of the elbow (<u>lateral</u> <u>ligament</u>): from the <u>lateral epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u> to the <u>radial notch</u> of the <u>ulna</u> and the <u>annular ligament of the radius</u> (<u>proximal radioulnar joint</u>)

* Ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow (internal <u>ligament</u>): from the <u>medial epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u> to the <u>coronoid process</u> and <u>olecranon</u> of the <u>ulna</u>

* Annular ligament of the radius (ring-shaped <u>ligament</u>): surrounds the <u>head of the radius</u> and anchors the <u>radial head</u> to the <u>radial notch</u> of the <u>ulna</u>

* <u>Carrying angle</u>: : measured using the axis of the <u>humerus</u> and the axis of the fully extended, <u>supinated</u> forearm (normally 5–15°)

* Movements  

* <u>Flexion</u> and extension

* The <u>concave</u> <u>radial head</u> can pivot on the <u>convex</u> <u>capitulum</u>, which allows forearm <u>pronation</u> and <u>supination</u> at the <u>radioulnar joint</u>.

* Blood supply: elbow anastomosis (an arterial <u>anastomosis</u> between branches of the <u>brachial artery</u>, <u>deep brachial artery</u>, <u>radial artery</u>, <u>ulnar artery</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Radial head subluxation</u> (<u>nursemaid elbow</u>), partial <u>subluxation of the radial head</u> at the <u>radiohumeral joint</u>, is caused by excessive axial <u>traction</u>. It is the most common <u>elbow</u> injury in children < 5 years of age.

## Cubital fossa (antecubital fossa)

* Definition: <u>triangular space</u> on the <u>anterior</u> aspect of the <u>elbow joint</u>

* Boundaries

* Laterally: <u>medial</u> border of the <u>brachioradialis</u>

* Medially: <u>lateral</u> border of the <u>pronator teres</u>

* Superiorly: imaginary line between the <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral epicondyles</u> of the <u>humerus</u>

* Inferiorly: <u>brachial artery</u> (dividing into <u>radial artery</u> and <u>ulnar artery</u>)

* Floor: <u>brachialis</u> and supinator muscles

* Roof

* Bicipital aponeurosis: a fan-shaped <u>connective tissue</u> sheath that connects the <u>biceps</u> <u>tendon</u> to the <u>ulna</u>

* Median cubital vein: a <u>superficial vein</u> of the <u>cubital fossa</u> that connects the cephalic and <u>basilic veins</u>

* <u>Medial</u> and <u>lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm</u>

* Contents

* From <u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>: <u>radial nerve</u>, <u>biceps</u> <u>tendon</u>, <u>brachial artery</u>, and <u>median nerve</u>

* Epitrochlear lymph nodes (<u>cubital lymph nodes</u>) [[3]](/library/wjYhc6)

* Located in the <u>subcutaneous fat</u> just above the <u>medial epicondyle</u> of the <u>humerus</u>

* Drains the ulnar side of the forearm and hand





> [!TIP]
> The <u>median cubital vein</u> of the <u>antecubital fossa</u> is one of the most common sites for peripheral <u>venipuncture</u> and <u>intravenous access</u>.




> [!TIP]
> The <u>epitrochlear lymph nodes</u> are classically enlarged in <u>syphilis</u> and/or <u>sarcoidosis</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> “Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest:” the contents of the <u>cubital fossa</u> are (from <u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>) Radial Nerve, Biceps Tendon, Brachial Artery, and Median Nerve.




References:[[4]](/library/ES08Yf)
